# Bloom composite cost, three cuts (Problem 2)

## MEASURED A/B (2026-09-01, runtime-patched live page, SwiftShader; gains in ms per frame vs same-load baseline; 4x = CPU-throttled weak-machine proxy; control drift 0.4ms at 1x, 0.04ms at 4x)

- Option C cheap-bleed: **the best bloom cut** - +0.48 (1x) / +1.25 (4x).
- Option B single-sheet: +0.55 (4x); the 1x pair read +3.1 but off an elevated baseline, treat 0.5-1ms as the honest size.
- Option A merge-copy: +0.14 (1x) / +0.38 (4x) - marginal; the pyramid was already cheap.
- A+B together: +0.77 / +0.28 - no super-additivity; the composite full-res fetches dominate what remains.

---


Proposal doc for `redesign-lab/perf-diffs/`. Read files: `_javascript/shader/kawaseBloom.js`, `_javascript/three-shared.js`, `_javascript/three-config.js`. All options keep D23 (no bright pass, bloom is the lighting rig) and D24 (paper pays for the low resolutions) intact.

## Where the milliseconds actually are

MEASURED: at the About-page bottom view, bloom off gains 3.2 ms (1x) / 6.7 ms (4x), paper off gains 4.4 ms; the full-res composite is ~89% of the pass's texture-fetch cost.

Counting fetches in the code (MEASURED from the shader, `kawaseBloom.js:148-183`): with paper on, the composite does **6 full-resolution fetches per pixel**: the two glow bands (`tMipTight`, `tMipWide`, lines 148-149), the straight frame tap (`tDiffuse`, line 150), the two paper sheets (lines 157, 167), and a second `tDiffuse` tap at a displaced position (line 179). The four chain renders before it are all at quarter scale or below and together are the remaining ~11%.

So the lever is the composite's per-pixel fetch count, and the paper-off ablation (4.4 ms for its 3 fetches plus blend math) puts a rough price on one full-res fetch: **~1 to 1.5 ms at the bottom view at 1x** (INFERENCE from the ablation split; the displaced tap is a fetch whose position depends on another fetch's result, the slowest kind on a software rasterizer, so it likely costs the most of the three).

The options are independent; any combination works.

---

## Option A: delete the copy render (5 renders becomes 4)

The chain's first render (`kawaseBloom.js:327-329`) blits the frame into the `half` target, one fetch per texel, purely so the 5-tap downsample has a pre-averaged source. The downsample can read the frame directly if its tap offsets stay sized for the old half-res grid, which keeps the tap footprint per destination texel identical; only the resolution underneath the taps changes.

**Diff (`_javascript/shader/kawaseBloom.js`):**

Header comment, lines 12-17, becomes:

```
 * This is four renders over three targets, all at half resolution or below:
 *   1 down       frame    -> quarter   (5-tap, reads the frame directly)
 *   2 up         quarter  -> wide      (8-tap tent, stays at quarter res)
 *   3 up         wide     -> tight     (8-tap tent, back to half res)
 *   4 composite  base + tight*f0 + wide*f1
```

Delete `COPY_FRAG` (lines 50-54) and the `this.copy` material (lines 214-218). The D23 rationale is safe: the "no bright pass" note lives in the header at lines 19-21, not in the deleted block.

Line 280:
```js
// before
this.quad = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2, 2), this.copy);
// after
this.quad = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2, 2), this.down);
```

setSize, lines 289 and 294:
```js
// before
[this.half, this.quarter, this.wide, this.tight].forEach((t) => t && t.dispose());
...
this.half = makeTarget(halfW, halfH);
// after
[this.quarter, this.wide, this.tight].forEach((t) => t && t.dispose());
...                                       // half target gone; halfW/halfH still size tight
```

render(), lines 327-335:
```js
// before
// 1. whole frame into the top of the pyramid
this.copy.uniforms.tDiffuse.value = readBuffer.texture;
this.blit(renderer, this.copy, this.half);

// 2. half -> quarter
this.down.uniforms.tDiffuse.value = this.half.texture;
this.down.uniforms.uHalfTexel.value.set(HALF_TEXEL / this.half.width, HALF_TEXEL / this.half.height);
this.down.uniforms.uTapOffset.value = tapOffset;
this.blit(renderer, this.down, this.quarter);

// after
// 1. frame straight down to quarter. Tap offsets stay sized for the half-res grid (tight has
//    those exact dimensions), so the reach per destination texel is unchanged; only the
//    resolution under the taps changed. The 0.5 pixel ratio and the paper grain cover the
//    undersampling this risks on tiny bright features.
this.down.uniforms.tDiffuse.value = readBuffer.texture;
this.down.uniforms.uHalfTexel.value.set(HALF_TEXEL / this.tight.width, HALF_TEXEL / this.tight.height);
this.down.uniforms.uTapOffset.value = tapOffset;
this.blit(renderer, this.down, this.quarter);
```

dispose(), lines 378-379: drop `this.half` and `this.copy` from the two arrays.

- **Predicted saving:** small. The copy is ~1% of the pass's fetches (MEASURED accounting), but each render on the software rasterizer carries fixed cost (target bind, state swap, full-screen quad setup). INFERENCE: 0.1 to 0.3 ms at the bottom view, plus one render target's memory gone.
- **Visual risk: subtle.** Each quarter texel now averages a 4x4 frame block through 5 taps instead of a pre-averaged 2x2; a 1-texel bright spark can slip between taps as it moves, so tiny bright features (firework sparks, the most distant lantern cores) may twinkle slightly in the glow. The 0.5 pixel ratio pre-blur and the 3.25 Hz paper boil mask exactly this. **Rod looks once at: distant lanterns and one firework over the water, watching the glow for twinkle.**
- **Line delta:** about -13.
- **Prefer when:** always; it is the free cleanup. Take it even if the saving reads as noise, because it is fewer lines, fewer renders, one less target.

---## Option B: drop the second paper sheet (one line)

The cold-press sheet (`tPaper2`) costs one full-res fetch plus the `blendSheets` math per pixel (`kawaseBloom.js:166-175`). The pass already has a wired-in off switch: `kawaseBloom.js:354` forces `uPaperMix` to 0 when no second texture is bound, and the `if (uPaperMix > 0.0)` branch is on a uniform, so the fetch and math then cost nothing. The shader keeps the two-sheet path for the lab tuner; only the live wiring changes.

**Diff (`_javascript/three-shared.js:72`):**

```js
// delete this line
bloomPass.setPaperTexture(paperLoader.load(`/assets/tex/${paper.sheet2}.png`), 1);
```

That is the whole change (and one texture download disappears from page load). If Rod locks it in, the follow-up cleanup removes the now-dead `paperTile2` / `paperMix` / `paperBlend` options at `three-shared.js:61-63` and the `sheet2` / `tile2` / `blend` / `mix` keys at `three-config.js:41-44`, about -8 more lines.

- **Predicted saving:** one of the paper's three fetches plus its blend math. INFERENCE from the 4.4 ms paper ablation: **~1 to 1.5 ms** at the bottom view at 1x, proportionally more at 4x.
- **Visual risk: visible.** The cold press at 4x tiling is the fine tooth INSIDE the washi fibre, and it is combined with SUBTRACT specifically so the field does not read as plain noise (`three-config.js:36-43`, Rod's bake of 2026-08-22). Without it the grain is coarser and softer at one scale only. This overturns an approved bake, so it is Rod's call alone. **Rod looks once at: the paper grain over the water and over flat sky, still and during the boil.**
- **Line delta:** -1 (-9 with cleanup).
- **Prefer when:** Rod judges the fine tooth is not earning a millisecond and a half, or as the reversible A/B test (re-adding the line restores the bake exactly).

## Option C: one displaced fetch instead of base plus bled

The ink-bleed (`kawaseBloom.js:179-180`) fetches the frame twice, straight and displaced, then mixes them 50/50 (`uPaperBleed * uPaperAmount` = 0.5 * 1, `three-config.js:45-46`). One fetch at the weighted midpoint approximates the same mix.

**The maths.** Exact: `E = (1-w)*f(uv) + w*f(uv+d)`. Proposed: `A = f(uv + w*d)`. First-order Taylor expansion of both around `uv` gives the identical value `f + w*(d . grad f)`; the difference is second order, `E - A = (w(1-w)/2) * (d^T H d)` with H the image's local curvature, zero wherever the image is locally a gradient, largest exactly at w = 0.5. In picture terms: the exact form is a shift PLUS a faint double image `|d|` wide (that double image is the "soak" look); the approximation keeps the shift, which is the part the boil visibly animates, and loses the doubling. Size of `|d|`: `slope * 0.0075` UV, typically 2 to 5 texels of the 642x402 buffer (the subtract combine can push rare texels higher), and all of it sits under the bilinear upscale to CSS pixels.

**Diff (`_javascript/shader/kawaseBloom.js`, composite `main()`, lines 147-188):**

```glsl
// before
vec3 glow = lerpBloomFactor(FACTOR_TIGHT) * texture2D(tMipTight, vUv).rgb
          + lerpBloomFactor(FACTOR_WIDE) * texture2D(tMipWide, vUv).rgb;
vec3 base = texture2D(tDiffuse, vUv).rgb;

if (uPaperAmount > 0.0) {
  ...
  vec3 bled = texture2D(tDiffuse, vUv + slope * uPaperDisplace).rgb;
  base = mix(base, bled, uPaperBleed * uPaperAmount);
  vec3 lit = base + glow * uStrength;
  gl_FragColor = vec4(lit + tooth * uPaperTooth * uPaperAmount, 1.0);
  return;
}

gl_FragColor = vec4(base + glow * uStrength, 1.0);

// after
vec3 glow = lerpBloomFactor(FACTOR_TIGHT) * texture2D(tMipTight, vUv).rgb
          + lerpBloomFactor(FACTOR_WIDE) * texture2D(tMipWide, vUv).rgb;

if (uPaperAmount > 0.0) {
  ...
  /* ink bleed in ONE tap: mix(f(uv), f(uv+d), w) matches f(uv + w*d) to first order, and the
     lost second-order term is a double image a few buffer texels wide, under the blur the 0.5
     pixel ratio already applies. Keeps the wobble the boil animates, drops the second frame
     fetch. Falls back to the straight tap as bleed or amount go to 0. */
  vec3 base = texture2D(tDiffuse, vUv + slope * (uPaperDisplace * uPaperBleed * uPaperAmount)).rgb;
  vec3 lit = base + glow * uStrength;
  gl_FragColor = vec4(lit + tooth * uPaperTooth * uPaperAmount, 1.0);
  return;
}

gl_FragColor = vec4(texture2D(tDiffuse, vUv).rgb + glow * uStrength, 1.0);
```

(The `...` paper-sheet block, lines 157-175, is untouched. The straight tap moves inside the non-paper branch, so the paper path drops from two frame fetches to one; the branch is on a uniform, so both paths still compile to a single fetch each.)

- **Predicted saving:** removes the displaced frame fetch, whose position depends on the paper fetch's result, the dearest kind on SwiftShader. INFERENCE from the 4.4 ms paper ablation: **~1 to 2 ms** at the bottom view at 1x, likely the biggest single win of the three at 4x.
- **Visual risk: subtle.** The bleed's faint double-exposure becomes a clean displacement; edges wobble the same amount but stop ghosting by a few pixels. Tuner semantics survive: `bleed` and `amount` still fade the effect continuously, they now scale the shift instead of the mix. **Rod looks once at: bright lantern edges against dark water, paused and during the boil, checking the ink-soak feel.**
- **Line delta:** about -2.
- **Prefer when:** you want the largest saving that touches neither the sheet bake (D24) nor the glow (D23). This is the one to take if only one is taken.

---

## Considered and rejected under D5

Folding the WIDE band into the final up-render (so the composite fetches one glow texture instead of two) saves a comparable full-res fetch, but needs two weight uniforms computed in JS plus either a second up-material or a branch in the shared one: net positive lines and a duplicated `lerpBloomFactor`. INFERENCE: ~1 ms for ~+10 lines. Park it; reconsider only if the bottom view still misses 60 fps after Problem 1's water options plus A and C land.

## Recommendation

Take **C + A** (about -15 lines, ~1.5 to 2.5 ms at the bottom view, both risks masked by the very softness the paper exists to own), and put **B** in front of Rod's eyes as a reversible one-line A/B before deciding, since it prices his own bake.
